newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan denies bombing northern Uganda.
newsitem.headline: Sudan denies bombing northern Uganda.

text.p: Sudan denied on Monday that its warplanes bombarded northern Uganda and said such claims harmed an agreement to normalise relations which both countries signed earlier this month.

"This news -- if really stated by the Ugandan state minister of defence -- is untrue," the official Sudan News Agency (SUNA) quoted General Mohammed el-Sanousi, spokesman of the Sudanese armed forces, as saying.
"It does not help the efforts of the two countries to consolidate the concepts of security specified in the recent agreement," he added.

Uganda's Minister of State for Defence Amama Mbabazi said earlier two Sudanese MiG planes had on Sunday dropped bombs aimed at an army barracks in the northwestern town of Moyo, 16 km (10 miles) south of Sudan's border but missed their target.
"It is true we have been bombed by Sudan...It is surprising that even before the ink dries on the agreement we signed they are bombing us," Mbabazi told reporters.
"We shall not sit back and watch while our territory continues to be violated. We shall soon respond appropriately."

Under the September 9 pact, mediated by Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on a visit to Khartoum and Kampala, the two countries agreed to work to halt activity by rebels in the border area. Both accuse each other of supporting rebel groups.
Sunday's air raid was the first since Sudanese planes bombed northern Uganda in January in an attack Khartoum said was aimed against southern Sudanese rebels.
"Two Sudanese MiGs came over on Sunday and dropped a number of bombs, around 10. Not all fell on Moyo and we have no reports of casualties," an aid worker, who declined to be named, said.

Other aid workers said they heard from the region that the MiGs attacked at 9:30 a.m. and dropped bombs and fired rockets at Moyo but no reports of casualties or damage were received, possibly as there were no aid agencies in the immediate area.
Sudan and Uganda had agreed to move any refugees and "hostile elements" at least 100 km (60 miles) from their common border, and to encourage voluntary repatriation of refugees.
The main southern Sudanese rebel group, the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), forecast on Monday the pact will not work because of Khartoum's "expansionist force".
An SPLA spokesman said the SPLA had no presence in Uganda so the raid was apparently a move by Khartoum to support the Ugandan rebel West Nile Bank Front, active in the Moyo area.

Mubarak al-Mahdi, leader of the main Sudanese opposition alliance based in Eritrea, had dismissed the pact as meaningless and said he believed Khartoum would keep giving arms to rebels of the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) fighting in northern Uganda and the SPLA would continue to have good ties to Kampala.
The LRA denies being armed by Khartoum and the SPLA denies being backed by Kampala.
The September 9 pact was also aimed at stopping the LRA taking refuge in southern Sudan and the SPLA taking refuge in northern Uganda.

Ugandan officials said there was no provision in the agreement for both countries to restore relations but said it included a foreign verification team to monitor the border area. Uganda broke relations with Sudan in April last year.
The SPLA has fought for greater autonomy or the independence of the mainly Christian and animist south of Sudan from the Moslem, Arabised north since 1983.
